item.title: WebLogic RCEs, AWS SSM Agent abuse, and Stadler/Nichirei extortion incidents
item.content:encoded:
Customer Advisory Kaseya VSA Ransomware Incident — Must Read

Kaseya VSA on-premises servers were exploited to push REvil/Sodinokibi ransomware to managed endpoints through a fake “Kaseya VSA Agent Hot-fix.” Affected MSPs and customers should shut down VSA servers, disable agents, block known IOCs, protect endpoint security settings, back up data, rotate credentials, and perform compromise assessments.

  • On July 2, 2021, Kaseya notified customers of a possible security breach in its Virtual System Administrator product.
  • Kaseya stated that victims were in the low thousands, while at least 36,000 Kaseya customers took their servers offline.
  • The attack affected MSPs using VSA to manage client endpoints, customers of those MSPs, and organizations using VSA to manage their own endpoints.
  • Attackers distributed an encrypted malicious file named agent.crt through the Kaseya VSA agent as an update called “Kaseya VSA Agent Hot-fix,” which was decoded to agent.exe and used in the ransomware attack.
  • The article recommends shutting down VSA on-premises servers, disabling VSA agents, blocking known indicators, backing up sensitive data, rotating credentials, and conducting compromise assessments.

Emerging Threat: Oracle WebLogic Server Multiple Critical RCE Vulnerabilities (July 2026 CPU) — Must Read

Oracle’s July 2026 Critical Patch Update fixes multiple critical Oracle WebLogic Server flaws, several of which allow unauthenticated remote takeover over exposed T3/IIOP, HTTP, SOAP, or SAML endpoints. Organizations should urgently patch affected WebLogic versions and restrict internet access to WebLogic listener and admin interfaces until patch status is confirmed.

  • Oracle’s July 2026 Critical Patch Update fixes multiple vulnerabilities in the Core component of Oracle WebLogic Server.
  • Five of the flaws have a CVSS v3.1 base score of 9.8 and allow unauthenticated remote takeover over T3/IIOP, HTTP, or SOAP.
  • The affected Oracle WebLogic Server versions are 12.2.1.4.0, 14.1.1.0.0, 14.1.2.0.0, and 15.1.1.0.0.
  • The article says any internet-reachable WebLogic listener should be treated as potentially affected until its patch level is confirmed against the July 2026 Critical Patch Update.
  • The article recommends inventorying WebLogic instances reachable from untrusted networks, restricting listener and admin access to trusted management networks, and monitoring logs for deserialization errors and malformed serialized objects.

Japanese food logistics giant recovers as extortion group claims cyberattack — Must Read

Japan’s Nichirei Logistics is restoring refrigerated warehouse and food delivery operations after a cyberattack disrupted supply chains nationwide, including KFC Japan. The extortion group RansomHouse has claimed responsibility and threatened to leak allegedly stolen confidential data, though Nichirei has not confirmed data theft.

  • Nichirei Logistics Group said it expects warehouse operations and frozen food shipments disrupted by last week’s system failures to return to normal by the end of the week.
  • RansomHouse posted Nichirei’s name on its dark web leak site, claimed responsibility for the attack, and threatened to release what it described as confidential data, projects, and documents.
  • Nichirei said some affected servers contained personal information and that it had notified the individuals concerned, but it did not confirm whether any data had been stolen.
  • The incident disrupted operations across Nichirei’s network of about 140 refrigerated distribution centers, affecting food manufacturers, supermarket chains, and restaurant operators in Japan.
  • KFC Japan said disrupted deliveries from a Nichirei subsidiary caused ingredient shortages at some restaurants, but later said deliveries had resumed and all restaurants had returned to normal operations.

Mitiga Security Advisory: Abusing the SSM Agent as a Remote Access Trojan — Should Read

Mitiga researchers showed that attackers with sufficient host privileges can abuse the legitimate AWS Systems Manager (SSM) Agent as a stealthy remote access tool, even controlling it from another AWS account or proxy server. Organizations should monitor for SSM re-registration, multiple agent processes, suspicious Session Manager activity, and avoid blindly allowlisting the SSM binary.

  • Mitiga discovered a post-exploitation technique in which the AWS Systems Manager agent can be used as a Remote Access Trojan on Linux and Windows machines and controlled from another AWS account.
  • The technique can affect EC2 instances as well as non-EC2 machines such as on-premises servers and virtual machines in other cloud environments that have an active SSM agent installed.
  • In one scenario, an attacker with root access on Linux or administrator access on Windows can hijack the original SSM agent by registering it in hybrid mode with a different AWS account.
  • In another scenario, an attacker can run an additional SSM agent process that communicates with the attacker’s AWS account while the original agent continues communicating with the victim’s AWS account.
  • Mitiga recommends monitoring for new SSM instance data directories, suspicious use of the amazon-ssm-agent registration flags, multiple amazon-ssm-agent processes, and suspicious Systems Manager activity in CloudTrail logs.

Swiss rail giant Stadler rejects $12.3M ransom demand after cyberattack — Should Read

Swiss train maker Stadler Rail says the Everest ransomware gang demanded about $12.3 million after stealing non-security-relevant technical data from a supplier platform. Stadler says its own IT systems, production, rail vehicles, and relevant personal data were not affected, and it will not pay the ransom.

  • Swiss rail vehicle manufacturer Stadler Rail said the Everest ransomware gang demanded 10 million Swiss francs, about $12.3 million, after breaching a data exchange platform shared with one of its suppliers.
  • Stadler said it will not pay any ransom and filed a criminal complaint with the Thurgau cantonal police.
  • Stadler said the incident occurred in mid-July and that its IT systems, production operations, and rail vehicles operating worldwide were not affected.
  • According to Stadler, the hackers stole only technical information from a supplier that was not security relevant, and no relevant personal data was stolen.
  • Everest emerged in 2020 as a ransomware operation but later shifted from encrypting networks to stealing data and threatening to leak it unless victims pay.

World Cup Retrospective: Analyzing the Surge in Cyber Threats — Should Read

Netskope observed a major spike in World Cup-themed cyber threats during the 2026 tournament, blocking more than 28,000 malicious attempts across over 1,000 organizations. Attackers used phishing, fake streaming sites, bogus job offers, and infostealer malware to exploit fan interest in tickets, streams, and FIFA-related content.

  • Netskope observed a spike in users attempting to visit malicious World Cup-themed content from the start of the 2026 FIFA World Cup through the end of the tournament.
  • At its peak, the number of users attempting to access malicious World Cup content was nearly six times the pre-tournament average.
  • Netskope detected and stopped more than 28,000 World Cup-themed threats across more than 1,000 organizations worldwide during the tournament.
  • Attackers used phishing and credential scams, including fraudulent job postings and fake videoconference pages, to trick users into providing account credentials.
  • Attackers also used fake streaming websites and file-based malware that promised World Cup tickets or match streams to support scams and deliver commodity infostealers.

Ransomware Strikes Azure Storage: Are You Ready? — May Read

Azure Storage accounts are a growing ransomware target because attackers can use stolen access keys or overly broad RBAC permissions to encrypt, delete, or overwrite cloud data. Organizations should reduce key-based access, enforce least privilege, restrict network access, monitor storage logs for suspicious read/write/delete patterns, and enable backups or blob versioning for recovery.

  • Sophos X-Ops observed the BlackCat/ALPHV ransomware group using a new Sphinx encryptor variant to encrypt Azure storage accounts with stolen Azure Storage account keys.
  • Azure Storage account access can be obtained through accounts with sufficient RBAC roles or through roles that allow Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/listKeys/action to list storage account keys.
  • After gaining access, attackers can encrypt storage data by mass downloading objects, encrypting them locally, and re-uploading them, or by using Azure Key Vault to generate an encryption key for blob storage or file shares and then deleting the key.
  • The article recommends monitoring Azure subscription activity logs and blob resource logs for actions such as enabling storage account key access, disabling blob versioning, deleting blob versions, and high-volume StorageRead followed by StorageWrite activity.
  • The article recommends limiting network access, using managed identities and Azure RBAC, rotating access keys regularly, and enabling Azure Blob Backup or Blob Versioning to help prevent and recover from ransomware attacks on Azure Storage accounts.

French Parliament greenlights social media ban for under-15s — May Read

France has passed a law banning social media access for children under 15, with new account restrictions starting September 1 and enforcement on existing accounts in January 2027. The move is part of a broader global push to restrict minors online, but critics warn age verification raises privacy concerns and blanket bans may not address harmful platform design.

  • Both houses of the French Parliament voted to block social media access for children under 15, making France the first European country to enact such a ban.
  • The law will take effect on September 1, when users under 15 will no longer be able to create new social media accounts, and enforcement for existing accounts will begin in January 2027.
  • The legislation also bans the use of cell phones in high schools, while such devices are already banned from elementary and middle schools.
  • Privacy advocates have criticized the ban because all users will be forced to verify their ages to access social media, and platforms reportedly must have their age verification methods approved by France’s privacy regulator.
  • Critics including Amnesty International’s Agnès Callamard said governments should focus on regulating harmful platform features, such as engagement-based algorithms, rather than relying on blanket bans.

How AWS EKS Pod Identity Feature Enhances Credential Management — Optional

AWS EKS Pod Identity simplifies how Kubernetes pods get AWS credentials by replacing more manual IAM role-for-service-account trust policy work with managed pod-to-role associations. The key benefit is easier, more secure credential management for EKS workloads, especially when automating access to AWS services across accounts.

  • AWS announced the EKS Pod Identity feature at re:Invent to help connect EKS pods and workloads to AWS services and clusters in other regions and accounts.
  • The earlier IAM roles for service accounts method maps an IAM role to a Kubernetes service account through an OIDC identity and requires trust policy changes using sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity.
  • The article says the older approach can be difficult to automate because each desired service account requires a manually added section in the role trust policy.
  • In the author’s test, a pod and service account were associated with an IAM role through the new EKS cluster Access tab without adding the eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn annotation to the service account.
  • The article states that EKS Pod Identity injects AWS_CONTAINER_AUTHORIZATION_TOKEN_FILE and AWS_CONTAINER_CREDENTIALS_FULL_URI environment variables into associated pods so they can obtain credentials.

Google Workspace - Log Insights to Your Threat Hunt — Optional

Google Workspace logs can support effective Google Drive data exfiltration hunting, but investigators must account for missing fields like user agents, file paths, and anonymous access, and normalize complex event structures. Key detections include unusual download/view/print activity, external sharing changes, third-party app activity, and reconstructing file paths from add_to_folder events to validate suspicious behavior.

  • The article focuses on threat hunting in Google Workspace with a primary hypothesis of data exfiltration from Google Drive through activities such as mass downloads, file sharing, and third-party applications.
  • Google Workspace logs lack several important forensic details, including user agent information, file paths, and log entries for anonymous users accessing publicly shared links.
  • The authors recommend restructuring the event parameters and splitting chains of events into separate records to make Google Workspace audit logs easier to investigate.
  • The originating_app_id field can help distinguish activity performed by third-party applications from direct user activity and can reduce false anomalies caused by application-hosting provider IP addresses.
  • The authors reconstructed Google Drive file paths from add_to_folder events using doc_id, doc_title, destination_folder_id, and destination_folder_title to assess whether a mass download of about 15,000 files was malicious.

Google Cloud Platform Exfiltration: A Threat Hunting Guide — Optional

Mitiga shows how an attacker with limited GCP image access in one project and stronger permissions in another can copy Compute Images across projects, export them to Cloud Storage via Cloud Build, and move them to an external bucket. The key takeaway is that GCP Storage logging may not clearly distinguish metadata reads from downloads or reveal the external destination, so defenders should use VPC Service Controls, organization restriction headers, and anomaly detection on Get/List activity.

  • The article describes a GCP exfiltration scenario in which an attacker compromises Bob’s account, uses his access to view Compute Images in the Monstera Project, and leverages stronger permissions in the Cactus Project to copy and export those images.
  • The attacker recreates sensitive Compute Images from one GCP project in another project using a GCP CLI or Cloud Shell method that does not require granting roles in the source project.
  • After copying the images into the Cactus Project, the attacker enables the Cloud Build API and exports the Compute Images as objects into a Google Cloud Storage bucket.
  • The attacker then uses gsutil with the cp command and the -r flag to recursively copy the bucket contents to an external Google Storage bucket controlled by the attacker.
  • The article states that GCP Storage logs can show object get, bucket get, and object list events, but may not distinguish object metadata reads from downloads or show the external destination bucket during the copy.

Learn how ransomware attacks have changed — and how incident response must, too — Optional

Ransomware has evolved from simple data encryption to double extortion, where attackers also steal data and threaten disclosure. Incident response must now prioritize rapid forensic investigation, exfiltration assessment, containment of attacker access, and breach-notification risk management—not just restoring from backups.

  • Classic ransomware typically involves attackers gaining access to data, encrypting it, demanding payment, and providing decryption keys if paid.
  • Modern ransomware, also called double extortion ransomware, adds data theft before encryption so attackers can threaten to release sensitive information if the ransom is not paid.
  • Reliable, secured, and separated backups can reduce the impact of ransomware by helping organizations restore data during a crisis.
  • Incident response for modern ransomware must determine what data was accessed or exfiltrated, how the attack happened, and whether attackers still have access to internal systems.
  • Executives responding to modern ransomware must consider notification requirements, applicable regulations, reputation risks, public relations challenges, and whether paying the ransom is necessary or possible.

Who Touched My GCP Project? Understanding the Principal Part in Cloud Audit Logs – Part 1 — Optional

The article explains how to interpret GCP Cloud Audit Logs to identify which user, service account, or delegated identity performed an action. The key takeaway is that fields like authenticationInfo.principalEmail, serviceAccountKeyName, and serviceAccountDelegationInfo are essential for tracing service account activation, impersonation, and delegation chains during investigations.

  • GCP Cloud Audit Logs include Admin Activity, System Event, Data Access, and Access Transparency logs, and the article focuses on Admin Activity and Data Access logs for forensic investigation.
  • Audit logs record the identity of the entity performing operations on a Google Cloud resource in the authenticationInfo field, which can include principalEmail, serviceAccountKeyName, serviceAccountDelegationInfo, thirdPartyPrincipal, and principalSubject.
  • The article identifies four main identity types in GCP: users, service accounts, service agents, and workload identities.
  • Service accounts can be activated with a private key file or impersonated for specific actions, and these uses appear differently in GCP audit logs.
  • For service account delegation chains, the operation appears as if it was performed by the last service account in the chain, while the full chain can be viewed in authenticationInfo.serviceAccountDelegationInfo.

How CEOs Can Embrace ‘The Cloud’ Without Compromising Security — Optional

CEOs can adopt cloud platforms safely by treating security as a core part of planning, vendor selection, integration, and staff training rather than an afterthought. The biggest takeaway is to prepare proactively for cloud-specific risks like misconfiguration, access control issues, monitoring gaps, and shared responsibility with providers.

  • Adopting cloud-based platforms can improve cost management, communication, scalability, and other day-to-day operations, but it also creates security concerns around sending and storing data online.
  • The article says organizations should prepare proactively for cloud security challenges such as misconfiguration, limited access privileges, poor password health, weak monitoring, link sharing risks, and targeted cyber attacks.
  • The article advises leaders to consider security responsibilities and costs when choosing a cloud platform, including which tasks belong to the organization and which belong to the cloud security provider.
  • The article states that using fewer cloud platforms may reduce security incidents because working with many vendors creates more opportunities for security compromise.
  • The article recommends training security teams, carefully planning cloud integration with legacy systems, and working with a trusted partner such as Mitiga for cloud incident readiness and response.

How enterprise GenAI can amplify ransomware risk — and how to contain it — Optional

Enterprise GenAI can amplify ransomware risk when compromised identities or over-permissioned AI assistants and agents give attackers faster access to sensitive data and business systems. Organizations should manage AI like any other high-risk enterprise workflow, with least privilege, monitoring, data controls, and human approval for risky actions.

  • The article says generative AI does not create an entirely new ransomware threat, but it can amplify existing attacker techniques such as reconnaissance, credential abuse, and data theft.
  • Enterprise AI assistants and agents can introduce risk because they may inherit user or service-account identities and delegated permissions for document repositories, SaaS applications, collaboration platforms, and internal knowledge bases.
  • Attackers who compromise identities tied to enterprise AI systems could use AI assistants to locate sensitive information more quickly or abuse AI agents’ permissions to export files, send emails, or invoke business tools.
  • The article cites examples of AI being used to support cyber operations, including GTG-2002 using AI for scripts and credential harvesting, GLOBAL GROUP using an AI chatbot for ransom negotiations, and a Chinese state-sponsored group using agentic AI in espionage activity.
  • The article recommends controls such as maintaining an AI application inventory, applying least privilege, monitoring AI activity, controlling AI-related data movement, preparing containment and recovery procedures, and requiring human or policy-based approval for high-risk actions.

Why Visibility Drives Everything in Modern Cybersecurity with Sevco’s Greg Fitzgerald — Optional

Sevco Security co-founder Greg Fitzgerald argues that modern cybersecurity depends on complete, real-time visibility across devices, users, apps, cloud assets, and vulnerabilities. The key takeaway is that organizations should correlate and normalize data from existing tools to prioritize the risks that matter most and automate response.

  • Greg Fitzgerald says Sevco Security focuses on cybersecurity visibility because many companies do not know all of their devices, users, applications, or vulnerabilities.
  • Fitzgerald says modern environments have become harder to manage because more devices connect to networks, users can download applications, access rights have expanded, and third-party supply chains are connected.
  • Sevco integrates through APIs with tools such as EDR, IAM, MFA, vulnerability scanners, Active Directory, network monitors, SIEMs, and SOARs to deduplicate, normalize, enrich, and share data.
  • Fitzgerald says vulnerability prioritization should use context, such as whether affected software is actually present and patched in an organization, rather than relying only on severity scores.
  • The discussion states that enriched asset and vulnerability data can help SOC analysts prioritize alerts, support compliance with NIST and MITRE ATT&CK models, and reduce risks related to fines, insurance issues, or legal liability.

Securing Claude: How AppOmni brings enterprise-grade governance to Anthropic’s AI platform — Optional

AppOmni is positioning Claude as a business-critical SaaS and AI platform that needs enterprise-grade governance, visibility, and threat detection. Its Claude connector monitors configuration, identities, permissions, and activity across Claude, Claude Code, and Cowork to reduce risks from misconfigured or unmanaged AI agents.

  • Anthropic’s documentation describes Claude as a platform that stores enterprise content, manages user access controls, exposes organization settings through an API, and supports agents that take actions across files, browsers, tools, and connected systems.
  • The article says many organizations are adopting Claude faster than they are adding oversight, creating a gap in centralized inventory and governance for agents.
  • AppOmni says it converts Claude enterprise data, settings, role-based access controls, and activity events into continuous posture checks, identity insights, and threat detection signals.
  • AppOmni’s Claude connector supports Claude Enterprise environments across Claude, Claude Code, and Cowork where Anthropic exposes organization settings and activity events through APIs.
  • For posture management, AppOmni runs Claude organization settings against an installable baseline policy with 24 rules and 9 Insights.

New InfraTrust report reveals infrastructure flaws admins should patch first — Optional

Eclypsium’s new InfraTrust Pulse report urges admins to prioritize patching internet-exposed infrastructure flaws that are actively exploited or remotely exploitable without authentication, rather than relying on CVSS scores alone. Top priorities include SonicWall SMA1000, Fortinet FortiSandbox, Dell networking, F5 BIG-IP, Juniper Junos OS, and NVIDIA BlueField/ConnectX issues.

  • Eclypsium launched InfraTrust, an infrastructure cybersecurity knowledge base, along with a monthly InfraTrust Pulse report to help organizations prioritize vulnerabilities in infrastructure, firmware, networking, and edge devices.
  • The inaugural July 2026 InfraTrust Pulse tracked 61 infrastructure advisories from 14 vendors, including six critical advisories and 26 remotely exploitable, unauthenticated vulnerabilities.
  • Eclypsium says administrators should prioritize vulnerabilities based on exploitability, reachability, exposure, and real-world risk rather than CVSS severity scores alone.
  • The report highlights SonicWall SMA1000, Fortinet FortiSandbox, Dell Networking, F5 BIG-IP, Juniper Junos OS, and NVIDIA BlueField and ConnectX advisories as patch priorities because they affect exposed infrastructure, are actively exploited, or can be compromised remotely without authentication.
  • The article notes that Russian and Chinese state-sponsored threat actors have increasingly targeted vulnerable network edge devices, including routers, VPNs, firewalls, and other internet-facing infrastructure.

From Breach Response to Platform Powerhouse: Ofer Maor on Building Mitiga for Cloud, SaaS, and Identity Security — Optional

Mitiga co-founder and CTO Ofer Maor explains how the company evolved from cloud incident response services into a platform for cloud, SaaS, and identity detection and response. The key takeaway is that effective cloud breach response depends on collecting the right telemetry in advance and using automation and AI to help SOC teams investigate faster.

  • Mitiga was founded to change incident response for cloud environments after its founders concluded that the traditional model of bringing in hourly response teams was outdated for modern cloud-based breaches.
  • Ofer Maor said cloud investigations depend on telemetry because organizations do not own or directly access the underlying cloud machines, and that telemetry is not enabled by default and often has poor retention.
  • Mitiga built its own data lake after finding that Splunk was not suited to the scale and cost profile of collecting large volumes of cloud telemetry.
  • The company expanded from cloud incident response into detection across cloud, SaaS, and identity because attackers move wherever access allows them, especially through federated identity and single sign-on.
  • Maor said Mitiga uses automation and AI to reduce alert triage time, with AI Insights and an automated triage analyst designed to help analysts assess alerts much faster.

Shadow AI Detection: See and Govern AI Traffic | Corelight — Optional

Corelight is promoting Shadow AI Detection, a capability intended to help organizations identify and govern unauthorized AI tool usage across network traffic. The main takeaway is that security teams need visibility into “shadow AI” activity to manage data exposure and policy risks.

  • The article is titled “Shadow AI Detection: See and Govern AI Traffic.”
  • The article is associated with Corelight.
  • The article focuses on detecting shadow AI activity.
  • The article presents visibility into AI traffic as a central topic.
  • The article presents governance of AI traffic as a central topic.
